text:
alex_k: Quick check — follow-up on the residency handoff prototype I landed yesterday. Seeing p99 tail regressions for small-batch chat (1-4 tokens). Anyone else seeing this?

maria_s: I saw a blip in the dashboards this morning, but didn’t dig in. Can you paste the p99/mean numbers? :eyes:

alex_k: baseline before patch: p50=12ms, p95=25ms, p99=48ms. after patch: p50=13ms, p95=27ms, p99=92ms. repro on dedicated staging.

alex_k: core diff is the handoff path where we return a residency token immediately and do async page-writes for host-backed pages. suspecting contention around the async handoff queue.

tanvi: hypothesis: async-write worker pool is starved and stalls a subsequent microbatch that needs the same page. small batches amplify. did you check worker queue depth?

alex_k: queue depth spikes to 1024 occasionally. single worker pool for all tenants.

ravi: can you try turning on the new per-tenant handoff cap? that was added in the earlier cleanup PR. should limit concurrent async handoffs per tenant to 8.

alex_k: good call — repro script run with HANDOFF_MAX_CONCURRENT=8 showed p99 fall back to ~56ms. still higher than baseline but much better than 92ms.

sam: is there a backpressure path when queue is full? iirc we currently drop-to-sync which can block the request thread. if small-batch request hits that, it explains tail spikes.

alex_k: yes, code path is: if async queue full -> sync write on caller. here's snippet from logs showing the blocking event: ```
[2026-03-22 14:12:11.123] tenant=acme req=0x7f write_mode=sync duration_ms=120
[2026-03-22 14:12:11.245] tenant=acme req=0x80 resume after write
```

luis: dropping-to-sync seems like a heavy-handed fallback. maybe we should stromgently prefer bounded async + short-circuit eviction hints instead of sync writes. e.g. return a temporary "stale" residency + schedule a fast priority refetch for very small requests.

tanvi: priority refetch is interesting but introduces complexity for correctness (clients might assume residency guarantees). we could offer a transient stale residency only for low-latency path with explicit gating in runtime.

alex_k: for an immediate mitigation I can: 1) enable per-tenant caps by default 2) add a short non-blocking fallback that returns a soft-failure to caller (let caller retry or fall back to cheaper model) 3) instrument per-tenant queue latencies. any preferences?

maria_s: do 1 + 3 now. 2 is risky product-wise — need product buy-in.

ravi: agree with maria. Also add a metric for sync-write count (per-tenant) and p99 latency correlation. we need to quantify how often callers hit sync fallback.

sam: also add a small telemetry tag on the response so we can correlate whether that request used a sync write on critical path. simple boolean in trace.

luis: long-term: we should consider dedicated short-lived worker pools for small-batch chat (low-latency SLA) vs large-batch offline jobs. that isolates noisy neighbors.

tanvi: +1 for pool isolation. affordable if we do pool sizing driven by observed small-batch qps.

alex_k: plan: roll back only a bit — enable per-tenant cap, instrument sync-write count and queue depths, add trace flag. I'll open a follow-up PR with the metrics and non-blocking fallback as an experiment behind a flag.

ci-bot: deploy queued: 2 changesets (alex/residency-cap, alex/residency-metrics). staging will be green in ~6m. :white_check_mark:

maria_s: thanks. if staging looks good, let's gate canary to low-volume tenants first.

alex_k: will do. I'll post back with staging telemetry after the deploy lands.
